items.title: AI is not for luxury: balancing Chronos efficiency and Kairos experience
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to theorise how AI-driven acceleration reconfigures firms’ temporal assets, creating efficiency gains while destroying relational time (trust, loyalty, premium value), a hidden cost invisible to managerial accounting but acutely felt by customers. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-method dual-coding design combining qualitative coding of 2,000 reviews (from a 1.2 M Google Maps corpus across 10 luxury chains) with an automated Gemini natural language processing extraction. The comparative design developed temporal categories and validated brand-level friction patterns while proving human interpretation essential to detect Kairos deficits and distinguish intentional deceleration from service failure. Findings Systematic temporal fractures where AI acceleration destroys relational value. Five Strategic Temporal Archetypes (Decelerator, Bifurcator, Autonomy Provider, Fragmentor, Automator) represent distinct competitive positions on the efficiency-experience frontier. Research limitations/implications This study extends AI, service and organisational temporality research by conceptualising AI as a temporal agent and introducing Kairos deficit, temporal extraction and temporal co-destruction. It also demonstrates the value of dual-coding methodologies combining computational scale with qualitative interpretation. Future research should test Strategic Temporal Governance and its archetypes across sectors, cultures and longitudinally. Practical implications Organisations should move beyond efficiency metrics towards strategic temporal governance. AI deployment should distinguish contexts where Chronos optimisation creates value from those requiring Kairos, intentional pacing and relational attention. AI systems should incorporate temporal transparency and human override, while managers should recognise frontline resistance to acceleration as potentially valuable temporal mediation. Social implications AI-driven acceleration can reduce opportunities for reflection, relational engagement and meaningful participation. When organisational speed dominates, technological progress may privilege efficiency over human temporal needs. Recognising Kairos alongside Chronos therefore matters socially, helping preserve spaces for deliberation, care, relational attention and human override rather than assuming that faster interaction always represents social progress. Originality/value Introduces temporal reconfiguration and Kairos deficit as strategic constructs; develops qualitative coding and constant comparison for lived experience at scale; validates the qualitative–computational distinction through comparative dual-coding against automated LLM extraction; reframes AI implementation as competitive positioning, not operational optimisation.

items.title: AI Readiness Index in the Public Administration, Bulgaria 2026
items.abstract: The second national study, “Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index,” tracks changes in attitudes, knowledge, and practices regarding the use of AI in the Bulgarian public administration between 2025 and 2026. The data was collected from 5,475 employees at the central, regional, and municipal levels. In 2026, the overall Index score increased, with the administration remaining in the “capacity-building” phase. The most noticeable progress was in the practical use of AI and employees’ readiness to work with such tools. At the same time, the institutional environment is evolving more slowly. Limited access to approved tools, the lack of clear internal rules, and poor knowledge sharing continue to be major obstacles. The results show that the sustainable implementation of AI in public administration requires not only more skills and training, but also clear responsibilities, secure access, and mechanisms for institutional learning. The raw data from the study are available in the open research repository Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22026174.

items.title: AI Readiness, Perceived Utility, and Professional Integration among Medical Technologists in Cavite: A Socio-Technical Study
items.abstract: This study assessed the levels of AI readiness, perceived utility, and professional integration of artificial intelligence among medical technologists in selected clinical and hospital laboratories in Cavite and examined the relationships among these variables. Grounded in a socio-technical perspective that integrates the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the research employed a descriptive-correlational design. One hundred licensed medical technologists were selected through purposive sampling according to predefined inclusion criteria. AI readiness was measured with the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students, perceived utility with the Professional Impact subscale of the Shinners Artificial Intelligence Perception questionnaire, and professional integration with items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Respondents demonstrated high levels of AI readiness (mean = 3.60) and perceived utility (mean = 3.64), indicating adequate knowledge, technical skills, and positive perceptions toward AI use in laboratory practice. Professional integration was also rated high (mean = 3.61), although AI remained only moderately embedded in routine workflows and many respondents were neutral regarding the actual extent of use. Correlation analyses revealed very weak, non-significant relationships among the three constructs, indicating that individual readiness and favorable perceptions did not translate into greater professional integration. The findings suggest that organizational and contextual factors—such as institutional support, infrastructure, and policy implementation—play a more decisive role in AI adoption than individual-level attributes alone. The study recommends structured, hands-on AI training programs tailored to laboratory practice, clear institutional policies and protocols for incorporating AI outputs into diagnostic workflows, and future research employing probability sampling, multi-regional samples, and longitudinal designs. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 3 by supporting improved diagnostic capacity and laboratory-enabled clinical decision-making, and to Sustainable Development Goal 9 by examining the conditions required for sustainable adoption of innovative health technologies. It advances public-health and institutional sustainability by clarifying the socio-technical determinants that enable resilient, digitally enabled laboratory services in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: AI Tutors and Human Tutors in Online Universities: A Critical Narrative Review of Replacement, Partnership, and Pedagogical Risk
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly proposed as a way to extend feedback, practice, and learner support in online universities. This critical narrative review examines the replacement, partnership, and pedagogical-risk claims made for AI tutoring. It synthesises foundational evidence on intelligent tutoring systems, recent evaluations of generative-AI tutoring, research on teaching and social presence in online learning, and current educational-governance guidance. The evidence does not support a general claim that AI tutors can replace human tutors. Structured intelligent tutoring systems have often outperformed conventional instructional comparators, but results against individual human tutoring are mixed and depend on subject, comparison condition, outcome measure, and implementation. Recent generative-AI studies show promise in carefully engineered, bounded learning tasks; they do not establish effectiveness for generic chatbots or whole-programme substitution. A partnership model is therefore more defensible when it assigns AI bounded roles in practice, preliminary feedback, and pattern detection while retaining human accountability for pedagogical design, consequential decisions, exception handling, and community facilitation. The review positions ENGAGE—Engage, Navigate, Guide, Articulate, Gather, Evolve—as a design-and-governance framework that translates those principles into an iterative course-level cycle. It also distinguishes documented capability and governance concerns from broader claims that remain plausible but under-tested, including cognitive deskilling. For online-university leaders, the practical question is not whether to automate tutoring wholesale, but how to design, disclose, evaluate, and govern hybrid configurations that improve learning without displacing educational responsibility.

items.abstract: THE INVARIANT SCRIPT AND THE STAGE : To the chief executives, venture capitalists, and algorithmic architects currently orchestrating the landscape of artificial intelligence: you are not the authors of the play; you are simply transient actors who have been handed a very loud microphone. On the contemporary stage of global capital, you wear the robes of a king. You command data centers that consume the energy of small nations, deploy models that alter human cognition, and witness financial valuations that mirror the GDP of empires. This unprecedented accumulation of wealth, physiological optimization, and political access creates a dangerous psychological feedback loop: the illusion of absolute autonomy. However, when the theatre curtains fall, the executive is stripped of the costume. In the sweeping scope of the cosmos, the most powerful tech leader remains a fragile, dependent speck of life—breathing air they did not engineer, occupying a body they cannot permanently preserve, and standing completely subservient to the ultimate power of the universe. On the stage you are a king, but in reality, you are a small human being.

items.title: AI versus human coding of NIH grant abstracts
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for qualitative analysis in substance use research, yet their performance relative to human coders remains underexplored. This study compares ChatGPT-4.0 with human coders in performing qualitative coding tasks using NIH grant abstracts as a test case, focusing on the identification and description of research innovations. Using a sample of NIH HEAL Initiative grant abstracts related to opioid overdose prevention, a total of 125 abstracts were independently coded by ChatGPT and humans to generate innovation descriptions, which were then evaluated by both human raters and ChatGPT for depth/detail and relevance/completeness using 5-point Likert scales. Identical instructions were used across all coding and evaluation stages. ChatGPT-generated descriptions were consistently rated higher than human-generated descriptions on both dimensions. Human evaluators rated ChatGPT outputs at an average of 4.47 for both depth/detail and relevance/completeness, compared to 3.33 and 3.24 for human outputs, respectively (F(1,176)=133.9, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that LLMs, when carefully prompted, can enhance the efficiency and quality of qualitative research evaluation.

items.title: AI-Accelerated Gyrokinetic Predictions of Turbulent Transport for Stellarator Design Optimization and Experimental Planning
items.abstract: Abstract Previous work built AI-based surrogates for a nonlinear gyrokinetic simulation code with the goal of using them for fast, direct calculations of turbulent ion heat flux in stellarator design optimizations and scenario planning for experiments. These AI surrogates were trained on data from \textgreater{}200k nonlinear, adiabatic electron gyrokinetic simulations with the gyrokinetic flux-tube code GX, using a wide range of stellarator magnetic configurations ($\sim$23k), positions in the plasma, and gradient scale lengths. In this paper, we demonstrate the use of the AI-based turbulence surrogate in the optimization of stellarator magnetic equilibrium and to speed up stellarator transport solvers. Due to its speed ($\sim${}ms), the AI-based surrogate enables previously unattainable optimization objectives, such as full radial profiles of ion turbulent heat flux, or directly optimizing to maximize the turbulent critical gradient at multiple locations across the plasma. These direct calculations provide a potentially more accurate optimization target and reduce reliance on ad-hoc heuristics that may not accurately capture the variation of turbulent transport with magnetic configuration. By including the AI-based surrogate for turbulent heat flux in a transport solver, we can quickly postprocess and confirm the improved ion temperature resulting from the optimized equilibrium. Finally, we demonstrate the use of AI agents with strong reasoning AI models to automate the outer loop, exploring many objective and hyperparameter configurations with this AI-based turbulence surrogate to discover improved turbulence optimized magnetic equilibria.

items.title: AI-Assisted Carotid Ultrasound for Nonexpert Use in Primary Care Cardiovascular Prevention: User-Centered Iterative Development Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Carotid ultrasound is traditionally confined to specialist settings because examination quality and diagnostic reliability are highly dependent on the operator’s technical skill and experience. Recent advances in AI-assisted ultrasound may enable task shifting to primary care staff and support the integration of personalized visual risk communication into routine preventive care. Visualization of subclinical atherosclerosis has been shown to strengthen cardiovascular risk communication and support preventive engagement. However, limited evidence exists on how such technology can be practically integrated into routine primary care workflows and what conditions are required to support use by nonexpert operators. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to describe an iterative user-centered design process enabling nonexpert use of AI-assisted carotid ultrasound for visualizing subclinical atherosclerosis in primary care cardiovascular disease prevention. METHODS We conducted a user-centered, iterative study within the Västerbotten Intervention Programme in northern Sweden. Fourteen nurse assistants from 4 primary care centers representing urban, rural, and remote rural settings tested an AI-assisted carotid ultrasound prototype with real-time guidance and artery segmentation in their primary care work environment, while 15 nurse assistants participated in semistructured interviews. Structured system-interaction observations were conducted during prototype testing. Interview data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke’s approach, while data from structured system-interaction observations were analyzed pragmatically to identify usability and workflow issues relevant to the iterative development process. RESULTS The thematic analysis of interview data identified 4 themes describing nurse assistants’ experiences and conditions for implementation: technology that fits the everyday primary care work; system guidance as a prerequisite for effective use; practical, peer-supported learning for confidence in clinical use; and confidence in the patient encounter. Observations identified recurring usability challenges related to ergonomics, probe handling, interface navigation, image acquisition, and time pressure. These findings led to iterative refinements, including redesigned interface navigation, simplified data entry, added audio feedback, enhanced probe support, and revised training materials. CONCLUSIONS This user-centered study identified key practical, organizational, and educational conditions for integrating AI-assisted carotid ultrasound into routine preventive care by nonexpert staff in primary care. The findings suggest that successful implementation will depend not only on technical capability but also on ergonomic and workflow fit, intuitive system guidance, peer-supported learning, and confidence in patient communication. These findings provide a foundation for future validation and implementation studies.

items.abstract: This record presents Version 0.9.0 of an open, non-peer-reviewed research artifact documenting the substantial use of an AI agent across an end-to-end educational research workflow. OpenAI Codex contributed to research-question generation, variable feasibility assessment, analysis planning, R and Python code generation, execution support, literature synthesis, manuscript drafting, validation, revision, and reproducibility documentation. The human researcher defined the overall objective, selected the research domain, directed the use of open R/Python methods, approved major workflow gates, requested sensitivity analyses and corrections, questioned the comparability of scores across TIMSS cycles, and authorized this public release. The AI system is not an author. Independent human verification of every analytical and interpretive claim has not been completed. The empirical workflow used Korean Grade 8 student data from TIMSS 2015 and TIMSS 2023. The recorded analytical environment used R 4.4.3 and Python 3.12.13, with random seed 20260802. Methods included weighted Gaussian latent profile analysis, TIMSS JK2 variance estimation, five mathematics plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules, BCH-type three-step correction, simulation and unit testing, sensitivity analyses, and an independent JK2 cross-check using the R survey package version 4.5. No commercial statistical software was required. A subsequent audit of official TIMSS documentation identified a critical measurement limitation. The 2023 metrics for Students Like Learning Mathematics (BSBGSLM) and Students Confident in Mathematics (BSBGSCM) were reset in 2023. Their 2015 and 2023 numerical scores are therefore not directly comparable. The Students Value Mathematics scale (BSBGSVM) retained the 2011 trend metric. Consequently, the cross-cycle profile means, shapes, and proportions reported in the included manuscript must not be interpreted as changes on a common 2015–2023 attitude scale. Item-level linking and multigroup measurement-invariance analysis are required before making such claims. The deposit includes the AI-generated manuscript, a Korean paper-development record, research-question materials, three sets of AI-agent instructions and prompts, R and Python code, aggregate analytical outputs, tables, figures, validation reports, failed-analysis records, approval and decision logs, software-environment information, file manifests, SHA-256 checksums, licensing information, and reproduction instructions. TIMSS student-level source files and row-level derived data are not redistributed. Third-party journal articles, TIMSS manuals and questionnaires, installed software binaries, model-object files, browser profiles, credentials, caches, and proprietary AI internals are also excluded. This record should be treated as an AI-assisted open research workflow demonstration and an object for reproduction, auditing, correction, and follow-up methodological research. It is not peer reviewed, is not a journal version of record, and is not represented as submitted to or accepted by any journal.

items.title: AI-Based Crop Disease Severity Assessment with Explainable AI: A Systematic Review of Methods, Trends, and Research Gaps
items.abstract: Crop diseases have a major impact on agricultural productivity and food security. Therefore, the timely detection and accurate severity assessment of diseases are of importance to effective crop management. Automatic crop disease detection and classification have been extensively implemented using artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning and computer vision. However, direct evaluation of disease severity and trustworthiness of model explanations are still important aspects to be explored. The review discusses recent progress on AI based assessment of crop disease severity and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI . Selected studies are analyzed based on type of crop and disease, datasets, AI models, severity evaluation methods, XAI methods, reported performance, limitations and gaps in research. The review explores various approaches such as convolutional neural networks, attention-based architectures, transformer-based models, segmentation techniques, hybrid frameworks, and few-shot learning. Approaches to severity assessment range from assigning diseases to predefined severity categories to quantifying disease severity and forecasting disease progression or related crop damage. We consider the utility of XAI methods such as Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients for interpreting model predictions and for identifying disease relevant regions or features. Furthermore, the review covers supporting studies regarding crop disease detection, classification, and risk prediction to comprehend their role and limitations for severity assessment. Several challenges are highlighted in the analysis including scarcity of standardized severity labeled datasets, inconsistent severity grading methods, limited crop and geographical scope, inadequate real-field validation, limited deployment of lightweight models and insufficient evaluation of explanation reliability. The findings highlight the need for robust AI models that can accurately assess disease severity and provide meaningful explanations across different agricultural settings. his review summarizes recent progress in AI- and XAI-based crop disease assessment, identifies important research gaps, and suggests future research directions toward the goal of building reliable, interpretable, and practical systems for precision agriculture.

items.title: AI-Based Student Performance Prediction Using Machine Learning
items.abstract: Student performance prediction is an important application of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. Academic performance can be influenced by attendance, internal assessment marks, assignment performance, study habits, previous examination results, and other learning-related factors. Traditional evaluation mainly depends on examinations and manual analysis, which may not i dentify students who require academic support at an early stage. This research proposes an AI-based student performance prediction system using machine learning techniques. The system collects relevant student information, preprocesses the data, selects useful features, trains machine learning models, and predicts expected academic performance. Algorithms such as Decision Tree, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine can be applied and compared. The models can be evaluated using suitable performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix. The proposed system can help teachers identify students who may need additional guidance and can support data-driven academic planning. The system is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for teachers. With reliable data and proper evaluation, machine learning can provide useful information for early academic intervention and improved learning support.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN ADVANCES IN CANCER DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT
items.abstract: Cancer is one of the most significant concerns of the health system in the world and early diagnosis and personalised treatment will be significant drivers in improving the outcome of patients. Cancer prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring are today an exciting area of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for cancer. Using AI, machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have the potential to capture tremendous amounts of information from clinical and imaging data, pathology, the genomic and molecular data. AI analysis of the CT, MRI, PET and histopathological images can aid in early diagnosis and the detection and classification of tumours. Precise oncology uses AI to integrate genomic information and clinical data and make precise, personalized treatment choices, patient categorization, prognosis of how patients will respond to treatment and predict whether they will return. AI is also playing a role in anticancer drug discovery in repurposing drugs, prediction of drug-target interaction and optimization of drug candidates. However, there are issues like robustness of data, privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, clinical validation and regulatory issues that need to be addressed. In total, the possibilities for AI to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, individualisation and patient-centredness of cancer treatment and care are huge.

items.title: AI-Driven Explainable Fake News Detection Using Large Language Models, Evidence Retrieval and Source-Aware Reasoning
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital media has made false and misleading information easier to create and distribute. Earlier fake-news detection systems largely relied on machine-learning classifiers, text vectorisation, and ensemble voting. Recent work has introduced BERT, large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a practical detector still needs reliable evidence, source awareness, uncertainty handling and understandable explanations. This paper proposes an AI-driven explainable framework that does not depend only on a trained classifier. The proposed system decomposes a news item into verifiable claims, retrieves supporting and contradicting evidence from multiple sources, evaluates source credibility and information freshness, performs semantic reasoning with an LLM, and combines the evidence into an evidence-weighted confidence score. Instead of forcing every input into a binary decision, the framework can return Real, Fake, or Uncertain together with the key evidence and a human-readable explanation. The paper presents the architecture, methodology, research gap, algorithm, evaluation plan and implementation design. The proposed approach is intended to improve transparency and robustness for both conventional misinformation and AI-assisted fabricated content.

items.title: AI–teacher collaboration: professional capital, cultural values and identity grafting
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how teachers with varying levels of professional capital respond to artificial intelligence (AI) collaborations, aiming to inform policymakers and school leaders about how to communicate change more effectively. We synthesize theories of professional capital, cultural values and identity grafting (IG) to develop propositions regarding teachers' willingness and ability to engage in AI–teacher collaboration. Specifically, the study analyses how professional capital (human, social and decisional capital) and cultural values (power distance, uncertainty avoidance and risk-taking) interact to shape teachers' IG processes (blending, balancing, repressing and reversing). Design/methodology/approach Drawing on international literature on AI in education and IG constructs as analytical tools, we conducted a secondary analysis to reinterpret our previously published cluster analysis results on Hong Kong teachers. Insights from this secondary analysis informed the development of theoretical and practical implications for future research and practice of AI–teacher collaboration. The process involved: (1) analysing how profiles of professional capital and cultural values from the published results might respectively indicate willingness and ability to engage in AI–teacher collaboration; and (2) theorizing with IG constructs how these patterns might indicate processes that will shape teachers' responses to AI–teacher collaboration. Findings High-professional-capital teachers, being less hierarchical and more risk-taking, are most likely to regard AI as a collaborator, blending their identities during human–machine collaboration. However, in terms of values, their aversion to power distance can lead them to reverse from AI adoption. Medium-professional-capital teachers exemplify the risk-averse middle majority who tend to avoid uncertainty and reverse from novel ideas. They may eventually form collaborative relationships with AI if authoritative agencies provide guidance regarding the benefits. Low-professional-capital teachers are highly likely to become risk-takers who disregard the intended outcomes of AI–teacher collaboration and remain skeptical of reform initiatives. Research limitations/implications This concept paper used our previously published results on teacher collaboration as the grounds for projecting how research on AI–teacher collaboration employing our proposed conceptual framework might look like. As the previously published results were meant to illustrate how the model we propose might link present research on teacher collaboration with future research agendas on AI–teacher collaboration, future research could validate the propositions presented in this paper with updated mixed-methods datasets directly related to AI–teacher collaboration. Practical implications The study offers practical implications for schools to sustain meaningful AI–teacher collaboration in nuanced ways. For high-professional-capital teachers, integrating them in professional learning communities can empower their social capital to co-construct AI–teacher collaboration with other teachers. For medium-professional-capital teachers, low-stakes participation and scaffolded entry into AI use can build confidence in this new knowledge base, promote trust in ethical AI use and ensure that AI usage is coherent with existing teaching norms. For low-professional-capital teachers, trust-building through inclusive yet careful scaffolding of low-stakes leadership opportunities may foster higher engagement toward AI integration and strengthen organizational change capacity. Social implications We offer initial insights into how teachers with different levels of professional capital might respond to calls for AI–teacher collaboration. To address concerns regarding the social ramifications of AI–teacher collaboration, changemakers must go beyond the adopter–nonadopter divide to understand the cultural values that underpin teachers' identity processes when interpreting change. Ignoring these differences risks dividing the teaching profession and the sustainability of AI–teacher collaboration. Initiatives that disempower, force consensus, promote distrust and exclude those who do not appear compliant bring diverse social ramifications, and our conceptual framework provides plausible indications of how they might manifest. Originality/value This paper proposes a theoretically novel IG approach to future research on AI–teacher collaboration, channeling existing research on technological adoption toward understanding teacher identity formations that underpin their willingness and ability to collaborate with AI (cultural values and professional capital). It provides tailored recommendations for policymakers and school leaders on professional development in AI–teacher collaboration for teachers with varied levels of professional capital, considering their cultural values and how they might respond to such support, given their IGs.

items.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports communication in healthcare by offering tools that simulate empathy and reduce patients’ sense of isolation, particularly in telehealth and senior care. Aim. The aim of this study was to analyze the mechanisms, opportunities and limitations of algorithmic empathy and digital empathy in healthcare, with particular emphasis on nursing practice. Methods. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (2020) guidelines. Literature searches were performed in the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and Google Scholar, covering publications from 2015 to 2025. Empirical studies, literature reviews and conceptual analyses addressing algorithmic empathy, digital empathy, socially assistive robots, and emotion recognition systems in healthcare were included. A descriptive synthesis was applied. Conclusions. Seven publications were included in the analysis. The results indicate that technological solutions may elicit responses perceived as empathic, which is associated with improved subjective well-being, reduced negative emotions and increased user engagement, primarily in long-term care, geriatric care and telehealth settings. Variability in intervention effectiveness and clinical context–related limitations were also noted. Algorithmic and digital empathy may support nursing care in conditions of limited direct contact. However, the use of such conditions requires professional oversight and a clear distinction between clinical empathy and technological solutions.

items.title: Algorithmic isomorphism and the erosion of competitive advantage in the age of artificial intelligence: A review of emerging risks in strategic management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is gaining prominence not only as an operational optimization tool, but primarily as a key element shaping decision-making processes and strategic management within organizations. The public and academic debate is dominated by concerns regarding job losses, privacy violations, social manipulation and biases hidden in algorithms. The purpose of this review paper is to transpose these issues into the realm of corporate management and examine a significantly less obvious threat: algorithmic isomorphism. This entails the homogenization of business strategies resulting from widespread reliance on the same global machine learning models. The article analyzes how the imperfections of artificial intelligence systems such as the lack of transparency (the black box effect), inherent database bias and their Western-centric nature can lead to the reproduction of identical market behaviour patterns. Furthermore, the impact of these technologies on the risk of unique know-how leakage and the loss of tacit knowledge held by human managers, which is crucial for competitive advantage, is discussed. The comprehensive analysis also encompasses the transfer of market mechanisms, known from algorithmic financial crises, to the sphere of long-term business decision-making. The conclusions point to the necessity of balancing technological innovation with a human-centric approach to protect corporate identity.

items.title: Algorithmic Management and the Erosion of Institutional Memory
items.abstract: This chapter examines how algorithmic management reshapes organizational resource management while weakening the human knowledge structures that support long-term adaptation. It focuses especially on the tacit knowledge risks that emerge when organizations rely heavily on data-driven managerial systems for coordination, evaluation, allocation, and control. Drawing on literature on tacit knowledge, institutional memory, organizational learning, transactive memory systems, hybrid governance, and human-centric AI, the chapter explains why institutional memory becomes vulnerable under datafied management. It argues that organizations face a dual challenge: they must benefit from AI-enabled efficiency without allowing managerial automation to erode tacit knowledge, mentorship, contextual judgment, and knowledge-sharing routines. To address this challenge, the chapter introduces a Hybrid Knowledge Governance framework and offers practical recommendations for more human-centered AI adoption.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Technostress, and Employee Mental Health in West Java
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of algorithmic management on employee mental health and the mediating role of technostress, viewing artificial intelligence (AI) as a double-edged sword in the workplace. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 300 employees in West Java, Indonesia, who had used algorithm-based work systems for at least three months and were selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.1. The structural model shows that algorithmic management has a significant direct effect on employee mental health and a strong effect on technostress, while technostress significantly affects mental health. The indirect effect through technostress is significant and accounts for about 61% of the total effect, indicating partial mediation. The model explains 78.3% of the variance in mental health and 64.7% of the variance in technostress. The findings show that algorithmic management can raise efficiency but also generates technostress that shapes employees' psychological condition. Organizations should combine AI-based control with human oversight, digital well-being policies, and technostress training. Keywords: Algorithmic Management; Technostress; Employee Mental Health; Artificial Intelligence; Mediating Effect

items.title: Amplifying Value Co-Creation in Small Family Businesses through Artificial Intelligence and Neuroscience: Twin Pillars for Intergenerational Decisions and Cohesion
items.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and neuroscience can jointly amplify value co-creation in small family businesses, whose competitive advantage rests on trust, close relationships and tacit, experience-based know-how transmitted across generations. The study combines a systematic literature review with narrative synthesis and conceptual model-building. Foundational sources were identified through citation tracking, and recent research was captured through a structured Scopus search (30 July 2026) that returned 296 records, of which 24 were retained after screening and quality appraisal and six further records were added through snowballing; a keyword co-occurrence analysis was performed on the full Scopus corpus. The review shows that AI acts as a strategic enabler rather than a mere automation tool, supporting efficiency, customer personalisation, innovation and intergenerational knowledge transfer, although recent evidence (2023–2026) indicates that its effects depend on the mode of family involvement, firm origin, organisational culture and governance. Neuroscience contributes insights into decision-making, creativity, stress and trust in emotionally dense family settings. The bibliometric map confirms that the two literatures have developed largely separately, as neuroscience terms are almost absent from the AI-in-family-business corpus. The article proposes a four-layer conceptual framework in which value co-creation mediates the effects of AI and neuroscience on organisational and family outcomes, moderated by firm-level, ethical and governance conditions, and formulates four working propositions for future empirical testing.

items.title: AN ILLUSION OF ENTREPRENEURIAL COMPETENCE IN ROBOTICS FOR SELF-RELIANCE IN KOGI STATE, NORTH-CENTRAL NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study critically interrogates the disjuncture between policy rhetoric and tangible outcomes in robotics-focused entrepreneurship development within Kogi State, North-Central Nigeria. Despite considerable public and institutional expenditure on robotics education, artificial intelligence infrastructure, and technology incubation schemes, the region exhibits a persistent failure to convert trained human capital into sustainable entrepreneurial ventures. Using a qualitative case-study approach grounded in secondary policy documents, institutional reports, and media coverage, the article argues that robotics entrepreneurship competence in Kogi State is largely performative symbolically enacted through official announcements and training certifications but materially unrealised owing to systemic infrastructural weakness, curricular irrelevance, institutional fragmentation, and deficient market linkages. Five interconnected obstacles are identified: erratic power and bandwidth availability; pedagogical models that privilege theory over practice; feeble university–industry partnerships; acute shortages of risk capital and accessible markets; and the absence of a cohesive ecosystem for technology venturing. The paper concludes by articulating a multi-pronged strategy to close the competence reality chasm, encompassing foundational infrastructure upgrades, curriculum overhaul, ecosystem orchestration, and locally attuned robotics applications. The analysis offers transferable insights for technology-entrepreneurship policy across sub-Saharan Africa, where similar mismatches between ambition and implementation are endemic.

items.title: Analisis Pengalaman Penggunaan AI dalam Pembelajaran pada Siswa DPIB di SMK Negeri 1 Singosari: Tinjauan Self-Efficacy dan Academic Dishonesty
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of experience using Artificial Intelligence (AI) on self‑efficacy and academic dishonesty among students in the Building Information Modeling and Design (DPIB) Expertise Program at SMK Negeri 1 Singosari. The study employed a quantitative explanatory approach, with a sample of 103 students selected through stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SEM‑PLS. The results indicate that experience using AI has a positive and significant effect on self‑efficacy, a negative but insignificant effect on academic dishonesty, and that self‑efficacy has a positive and significant effect on academic dishonesty. These findings emphasize the importance of utilizing AI coupled with digital literacy and ethical awareness in learning. In addition, the study highlights the relevance of integrating technological experience into educational practices, encouraging students to develop confidence, responsibility, and integrity. The implications suggest that schools should design programs that foster ethical digital skills and strengthen students’ readiness for future innovation.

items.title: APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ASSESSING THE EARTHQUAKE RESISTANCE OF BUILDINGS
items.abstract: This thesis examines the possibilities of using artificial intelligence technologies to assess the earthquake resistance of buildings. Earthquakes can cause cracks, deformations, displacements, and other types of damage to building structures. Since traditional assessment methods often require considerable time and human resources, the use of modern machine learning and computer vision algorithms is becoming increasingly important. This study analyzes the possibilities of using photographs and video data of buildings to automatically detect structural damage, assess its severity, and provide a preliminary evaluation of the building's seismic performance.

items.title: APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON MARKETING PERFORMANCE, GUEST SATISFACTION AND LOYALTY: IMPLICATIONS FOR SUSTAINABLE INTERNATIONAL HOTEL BUSINESS IN ABUJA, NIGERIA
items.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping hotel marketing and guest-service delivery, yet empirical evidence on its implications for guest satisfaction and loyalty in developing hospitality markets remains limited. This study examined AI applications in selected international hotels in Abuja, Nigeria, focusing on their perceived contribution to marketing performance, guest satisfaction and loyalty, as well as barriers to adoption. A cross-sectional mixed-methods design was employed, involving hotel staff and guests from six selected hotels. Data were collected through structured questionnaires, key-informant interviews and observation. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression and mediation analysis were used to examine relationships among the study variables. The findings indicate that conventional digital technologies were more widely used than genuine AI applications, with chatbots, machine-learning forecasting, intelligent recommendation systems and AI-supported analytics representing the principal AI-related applications. AI-supported guest experience was positively associated with satisfaction, while satisfaction demonstrated a stronger relationship with loyalty. The findings further indicate that cost, shortage of specialised skills, privacy and cybersecurity concerns, systems integration and infrastructural limitations constrain effective AI adoption. The study concludes that AI does not automatically generate guest loyalty; rather, its value depends on the quality, relevance and trustworthiness of the experience it creates. The study contributes by distinguishing AI from conventional digitalisation and proposing a human-centred pathway linking AI-supported experience, satisfaction and loyalty in the Abuja hospitality context.

items.title: Artificial gravity for long-duration human spaceflight: physiological rationale, evidence gaps, risks, and research priorities
items.abstract: Long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit will expose crews to prolonged microgravity during transit and partial gravity on the Moon or Mars. Existing exercise, nutritional, pharmacological, and sensorimotor countermeasures mitigate selected aspects of deconditioning but do not reproduce gravity’s continuous multisystem stimulus. Artificial gravity (AG), generated by rotation, is therefore a promising integrative countermeasure. This structured narrative review evaluates the physiological rationale for AG, evidence from human centrifugation and ground-based analog studies, human-factors and engineering constraints, and priorities for exploration missions. Evidence is strongest for the acute restoration of hydrostatic gradients and cardiovascular loading and is suggestive, although heterogeneous, for preserving orthostatic tolerance, muscle function, and selected sensorimotor outcomes. In the 60-day AGBRESA study (24 participants; eight per group), daily continuous or intermittent centrifugation attenuated the decline in time to presyncope relative to control but did not prevent several autonomic, ocular, balance, or mobility changes. Evidence for durable protection of bone, connective tissues, neuro-ocular health, immunity, endocrine and circadian regulation, cognition, sleep, and behavioural health remains insufficient. Interpretation is limited by small samples, overlapping cohort analyses, heterogeneous exposure geometries and schedules, and reliance on bed-rest analogs rather than in-flight trials. AG should therefore be regarded as a configurable intervention rather than a single countermeasure. Translation requires standardized reporting, adequately powered comparative studies, explicit safety and ethical governance, analyses of sex-related and individual responses, combined AG–exercise protocols, and phased validation from ground-based analogs to orbital demonstrators.

items.title: Artificial intelligence - driven toxicogenomics for predictive environmental and pharmaceutical safety
items.abstract: Toxicogenomics integrates high-throughput genomic technologies with toxicology to evaluate molecular responses to chemical and pharmaceutical exposures. The increasing volume and complexity of multi-omics data necessitate advanced computational approaches capable of extracting meaningful and predictive insights. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques—including support vector machines, random forests, and deep learning architectures—are increasingly employed for early toxicity prediction and risk assessment, with reported improvements in predictive accuracy and sensitivity relative to conventional toxicological approaches. This paper explores the role of AI-driven toxicogenomics in enhancing predictive environmental and pharmaceutical safety. It highlights the application of ML-based and data-driven models for the integrative analysis of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets to identify toxicity-associated biomarkers, elucidate mechanisms of action, and predict adverse drug and environmental effects prior to clinical manifestation. Notably, AI-driven models have demonstrated significant improvements in prediction accuracy, sensitivity, and scalability compared to traditional toxicological approaches, reducing reliance on animal testing and accelerating decision-making processes. Furthermore, the paper discusses the significance of AI-based toxicogenomics in drug development, environmental contaminant screening, and regulatory toxicology, while addressing key challenges such as data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. The convergence of computer science and toxicogenomics represents a robust framework for next-generation predictive toxicology, facilitating safer pharmaceutical development, more precise environmental risk assessment, and evidence-based public health and regulatory decision-making.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and digital technologies in public administration: a constitutional and legal dimension
items.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive constitutional-legal analysis of the use of artificial intelligence and other digital technologies in public administration. The study aims to define the constitutional and legal foundations for their application, identify key risks to human rights and freedoms, and substantiate a differentiated model of legal safeguards based on the intensity of digital influence on legally significant outcomes. The relevance of this issue stems from the gradual shift from using digital tools merely for technical support to employing them in processes involving data analysis, the formulation of recommendations, the determination of parameters for official decisions, and the automated adoption of legally significant decisions. The study employs formal-legal, comparative-legal, and system-structural methods, as well as the method of legal modeling. It analyzes constitutional principles and norms of national legislation, contemporary European and international approaches to the regulation of artificial intelligence, and the specific aspects of using automated systems in the activities of public administration. The article establishes that the constitutional and legal significance of digital technology is determined by the extent of its impact on the exercise of public authority and the legal status of the individual. It is argued that a digital system cannot serve as an independent source of public competence; rather, its software architecture and settings must comply with legally prescribed limits of authority and cannot effectively alter the substance of legal regulation. The article analyzes the requirements of legality, legal certainty, equality and non-discrimination, privacy protection, accountability, due process, and effective legal protection within the context of the algorithmization of public administration. The scientific novelty of the study lies in substantiating the principle that constitutional and legal safeguards should be strengthened in proportion to the intensity of digital influence. Building on this principle, the article proposes a four-level model of digital influence and develops a digital influence intensity test based on four criteria: the functional role of the system, the nature of the legal consequences, the characteristics of the data used, and the extent to which meaningful human review is genuinely available. The study further substantiates a set of safeguards applicable in cases of substantial digital influence, including the right to be informed about the significant use of artificial intelligence, a legally sufficient explanation of the decision, meaningful human review, a prior impact assessment concerning constitutional rights, digital auditing, and effective mechanisms for review and appeal. It is concluded that it is advisable to establish a differentiated model of legal regulation for the use of artificial intelligence in public administration in Ukraine, wherein the scope of legal safeguards is determined by the digital system's actual role in generating a legally significant outcome. This approach makes it possible to reconcile the efficiency of public sector digitalization with the requirements of legality, accountability, and adequate human rights protection, without imposing uniformly stringent regulatory requirements on technologies that have varying degrees of legal impact.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND GEOSPATIAL TECHNOLOGIES FOR WATER QUALITY MONITORING: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF TRENDS, METHODS, AND RESEARCH GAPS
items.abstract: Water quality monitoring is essential for ensuring the sustainable use of aquatic resources and preserving ecosystem health. The increasing application of artificial intelligence (AI) in this field has provided innovative approaches to modeling and predicting key water quality parameters with greater efficiency. This study aimed to map the landscape of scientific production, understand the correlation network among identified themes, and analyze the temporal evolution of publication output. We conducted a bibliometric analysis of scientific publications related to the use of AI in water quality assessment, employing tools such as Bibliometrix and VOSviewer. A total of 130 peer-reviewed articles were retrieved from the Web of Science and Scopus databases, covering the period from 2005 to 2025, and analyzed to identify research trends, key themes, and collaboration networks. Thematic clustering of keywords revealed four main research areas: (i) remote sensing, (ii) machine learning, (iii) water quality indicators, and (iv) hydrodynamic and watershed modeling. The results show that the term “machine learning” is central to the analyzed literature, connecting clusters focused on hydrological modeling, remote sensing, supervised learning algorithms, and the prediction of physicochemical variables. The findings highlight the interdisciplinary nature of the field and underscore the growing role of AI and geotechnologies as cost-effective tools for supporting water quality management, particularly in hard-to-access areas. These insights offer guidance for future research and help environmental agencies develop more efficient strategies for monitoring and preserving water resources.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Asthma Care in Nigeria and Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence, Opportunities, and Adoption Barriers
items.abstract: Asthma affects an estimated 363 million people worldwide and caused approximately 442,000 deaths in 2023. The burden of this disease falls disproportionately on low-income and middle-income countries where the disease is mostly underdiagnosed and under-treated. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have been presented as tools for earlier diagnosis, personalised treatment, exacerbation prediction, and remote monitoring. However, much of the supporting research originates from high-income settings. Our review evaluates what the supporting evidence offers for asthma care in Nigeria and the African region. We conducted a literature search across PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and similar databases, with the resulting review library consisting of 170 screened records. 116 records were reviewed in full, while 31 were retained for in-depth review of their techniques, data sources, algorithms, conclusions, and implications. Four themes emerged: an expanding but unevenly equipped African AI ecosystem; AI/ML tools for diagnosis, exacerbation prediction, and digital monitoring developed and validated almost entirely outside Africa; persistent non-technical barriers to asthma care in sub-Saharan Africa, including under-diagnosis, restricted access to medications, and insufficient awareness among carers and educators; and unresolved ethical, legal, and data governance issues. The reviewed studies demonstrate technical feasibility in high-income settings but reveal a lack of African validation. We conclude that AI and ML can enhance asthma care in Nigeria only if models are validated on African data, integrated into existing care frameworks, and governed by explicit regulations. We therefore propose seven recommendations for policymakers, clinicians, and researchers.
